sources.headline: Alaska Senate candidate denies knowing about alleged plot to put two Dan Sullivans on ballot
sources.text: Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola has denied she knew anything about an alleged "scheme" that led to two men named Dan Sullivan standing in the Alaska Senate race.The denial comes as the Trump administration continues to escalate a criminal investigation into the matter. The Republican governor of the state ordered an official inquiry earlier this week. Dan S Sullivan, the incumbent Republican senator running for re-election, and allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters.The Alaska race is considered by analysts to be one of the tightest of the upcoming US midterm elections, which will decide which party controls Congress."I just want to clear the air," Peltola said while speaking to voters on Thursday. "I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters."Both Dan Sullivans have been running for the open Senate seat for some time. Still, controversy erupted earlier this week when The New York Times, external reported that Peltola's team worked with people who tried to recruit spoiler candidates in the Senate race.The Times's report alleged that people connected to Peltola's campaign, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), worked to try to recruit Dan J Sullivan, a retired teacher who lives in a remote fishing village, to stand in the Senate race.The paper said it had seen text messages and interviewed 12 people who participated in or were told of the plan, or were would-be candidates who the team tried to recruit. The BBC has not independently verified the reporting.The Peltola campaign has denied those reports and Sullivan has denied any links to the campaign.But those denials have not stopped the justice department (DOJ) and Republicans from attacking Peltola. The DOJ has begun issuing subpoenas targeting Democratic officials allegedly connected to the effort to recruit Dan J Sullivan to be on the Alaska ballot, according to CBS News, the BBC's US news partner. No charges had been filed as of Friday morning. "There is both a civil investigation and a criminal investigation that are ongoing," Michael Heyman, the US attorney for the district of Alaska, said at a Friday afternoon press conference. Heyman did not immediately provide details of specific crimes his office would investigate.Scott Kendall, an attorney who worked with Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski in her 2010 and 2016 campaigns, told the BBC he was sceptical the actions described in the New York Times story broke the law.Alaska law does not have specific good-faith requirements for candidates, Kendall explained - noting that spoiler candidates sometimes emerged in their contests. "I freely admit there could be more facts, but I'm not going to speculate they exist," he said.The spectre of a federal crimes could come into play if there was potential evidence of campaign finance violations, Kendall, as well as other legal experts, told the BBC. But such evidence has not yet emerged.Kendall believed the primary risk to Peltola from the allegations is "absolute reputational harm". The Trump administration filed a federal lawsuit last week aimed at preventing the certification of the result if the Trump-backed Sullivan loses, arguing the presence of both of them on the ballot could confuse voters.On Wednesday, the justice department amended its lawsuit to include the reporting by the Times, citing significant sections of the story as well as Governor Mike Dunleavy's announcement of an investigation.A federal judge has expedited consideration and will weigh motions to dismiss brought by Alaska election officials and backed by the Peltola campaign and voting rights groups.The legal action comes days before voters across the US head to the polls. This race in Alaska is among the closest-watched in the country, as it could be the deciding factor in who controls the Senate. The non-partisan Cook Political Report currently classifies the race as a toss-up. As the final weekend of campaigning approaches, President Donald Trump will appear at back-to-back rallies in Kansas and Iowa on Sunday.The in-person appearances were previously cancelled, but a source familiar with planning told the BBC that they were rescheduled to accommodate remote appearances by Trump at tele-rallies.

sources.text:
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day. Today's top stories It is the final stretch before Election Day on Tuesday and candidates are making final campaign stops and delivering closing arguments. President Trump has been campaigning for at-risk Republicans, but he has abruptly switched to virtual rallies.
A person walks past a voting sign at the East Point Library on Tuesday, the first day of early voting, in Atlanta.

🎧 Trump's tour to boost voter turnout has focused largely on competitive Republican-leaning states, NPR's Saige Miller tells Up First. He's hosting 19 telerallies alongside in-person events. The shift in strategy, plus polling data, suggests that Republicans may face challenges, at least in the House, Miller says. Trump knows he's a key motivator for his party, but his strategy could also backfire by energizing Democrats.🎧 Alaska's governor has ordered an investigation following a New York Times report on the state's toss-up U.S. Senate race. The article revealed that Democratic campaign operatives were attempting to recruit a candidate, whom Republicans claim could confuse voters and siphon support from GOP incumbent Dan Sullivan. The candidate also shares the name Dan Sullivan. Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman, aims to flip the seat. Alaska Public Media's Liz Ruskin spoke with election law experts, who found no applicable laws but noted that the conduct described crosses moral and ethical lines.➡️ The Department of Justice subpoenaed election workers in Los Angeles amid rising tensions with California officials over the Trump administration's efforts to identify noncitizens on voter rolls.➡️ At the start of this election cycle, Democrats appeared unlikely to gain Senate seats because many races were in red states. But the ongoing war in Iran has changed the landscape. Here are the key Senate races to watch.➡️ NPR member stations are compiling essential info for voters, from guides to local races. Discover resources in your community here.➡️ The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has dismissed Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, who oversaw planning at the Pentagon. Sylvia was also part of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. His removal comes as the U.S. and Israel prepare for a new potential round of attacks against Iran. Although Sylvia held a senior position in strategy, planning and policy, he was not directly involved in day-to-day operations regarding the Iran conflict. 🎧 The Pentagon is investigating a leak but has not provided details, NPR's Greg Myre says. Hegseth has dismissed several generals and admirals, often without explanation. These firings have disrupted senior military operations, Myre says. The U.S. currently has two aircraft carriers in the Arabian Sea, with a third, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, en route. According to Myre, it is unusual for the U.S. to have multiple carriers in one region. The last time it stationed three in the Middle East was during the 2003 invasion of Iraq. Thousands of military veterans with VA-backed mortgages have faced higher interest rates and monthly payments since last year, after the Trump administration shut down a key part of the VA's home loan program. Before it was shut down, the Veterans Affairs Servicing Purchase (VASP) program, created under the Biden administration, helped tens of thousands of veterans who had fallen behind on their payments by rolling missed payments into a new, low-interest mortgage. The mortgage industry and housing groups warned the administration not to kill the program without first creating a viable replacement. Without one, vets had to modify loans at higher interest rates. An NPR investigation found that more than 15,000 veterans experienced monthly payment increases of at least $150 after their loans were modified due to financial hardship. More than 700 veterans saw their payments rise by $1,000 or more.
Behind the story by Rob Stein, NPR's science desk correspondent and senior editor
Mary Long/Getty Images
I've been doing stories about the organ transplantation system for decades. One of the most fundamental guiding ethical principles in organ donation has long been the "dead donor rule." That rule, stated simply, says: Organs should only be retrieved for transplants from a person who is dead, and death should never be accelerated to try to boost the chances their organs will be usable. To make sure that's the case, there's long been a strict firewall between the doctors and nurses trying to save patients in the hospital, and the organ retrieval teams standing by to try to procure their organs. But over the years, I've heard many stories from family members who nevertheless felt pressured to donate their loved one's organs. So when I got a tip that the Organ Procurement & Transplantation Network, which runs the nation's organ system, was planning to relax that firewall, I instantly knew that was a big story. I rushed to confirm the documentation that the network's board of directors had indeed endorsed the change, which would go into effect Nov. 18. I then reached out to bioethicists and others for their reaction to this major change. The revision was part of a set of new policies designed to boost donations and improve patient safety. Those changes were spurred by disturbing revelations about mistakes, including patients literally being wheeled into the operating room to remove their organs when they were still alive. Some of the changes were praised as improving safety. But many bioethicists and even some transplant surgeons and patient and organ donation advocates say relaxing the firewall between care and organ retrieval teams is dangerous. The fear is it could lead to families and caregivers discontinuing treatment too soon, and deepening distrust in the organ donation system.
I explored what these rule changes will mean for organ donors. You can read about it here. Weekend picks

sources.headline: Two Dan Sullivans are running in Alaska. Trump thinks one is a decoy
sources.text: Something fishy is going on in Alaska ahead of the midterms, but it has nothing to do with the state's famous seafood and everything to do with two men with the same name.Two Dan Sullivans are running for the US Senate on November 3.One is Dan S Sullivan, Alaska's Republican incumbent who is seeking a third six-year term. The other is Dan J Sullivan Jr, a retired elementary-school teacher who entered the race in May.When the two appear together on the ballot in print, Daniel J Sullivan is listed first, with no party designation, followed by Dan S Sullivan, registered Republican incumbent.A sample election ballot shows the two Dan Sullivans on the ballot. (AP: Haven Daley)US President Donald Trump isn't too happy about it."They [the Democrats] found a guy named Dan Sullivan. They put him up to get [voters] a little confused," he said at a rally for the Alaskan incumbent in mid-October.This week, he directed the Department of Justice to sue to block certification of the Senate race if Republicans do not win Alaska, believing Daniel J Sullivan is a "decoy" aimed at siphoning votes away from the Republican candidate.The top federal prosecutor in Alaska confirmed the existence of a criminal investigation on Friday, local time.Attorney Michael Heyman would not say what potential crimes authorities were looking into or the targets of the probe, but encouraged the public to come forward with tips that could help investigators.Republicans argue voters intending to vote for Dan S Sullivan may confuse him with Dan J Sullivan and accidentally select his name on the ballot. Some Alaskans have dismissed the notion, arguing they are smarter than the Grand Old Party (GOP) gives them credit for.The bizarre issue, which has been playing out for months, deepened on Wednesday, local time, when The New York Times reported the campaign of rival Democrat candidate in Alaska, Mary Peltola, had recruited Dan J Sullivan in an effort to dilute the GOP vote.Both Ms Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) have denied participating in such efforts.Dan J Sullivan has insisted he is running in good faith, saying his namesake is "making decisions that I don't think are necessarily moving our state forward". He has, however, acknowledged that having the same name as the incumbent has been a boon for his campaign."I knew that my name recognition would get me immediate publicity," he told The New Yorker in August."It's succeeded beyond my wildest hopes."The Alaskan campaign has now kicked up a debate about ballot stacking tactics, widely-watched US Senate races and Republican allegations of election interference just days before the midterms.A tale of two DansBack in May, the battle of the Dans came to a head when a top state elections official ruled Dan J Sullivan ineligible for the primary ballot.The official concluded Dan J Sullivan's declaration of candidacy was filed "with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot's fairness or neutrality".But the Alaska Supreme Court later overturned the decision, ruling he was qualified to run after finding the decision to strike him from the ballot was unlawful.US Senator Dan Sullivan is running against another Dan Sullivan in next week's midterms. (Reuters: Jacquelyn Martin/Pool)"It's all because of my name, and you know, there's nothing I can do about my name," Dan J Sullivan told a local news outlet after the decision."I was frustrated. I felt it's time for a change, and so I wanted to jump into the race and make my feelings and my thoughts known …They tried to make it more than that, and you know, that's their prerogative."It isn't the first time a candidate has run against a namesake in the United States, nor is it the first time Dan S Sullivan has run against another of the same name.When the Republican first ran for Senate in 2014, he appeared on the same ballot as Dan A Sullivan, the mayor of Anchorage, who had run for lieutenant governor.But Republicans think the presence of Daniel J Sullivan, whom they refer to as "Decoy Dan" or "Fake Dan", on this year's ballot is a Democratic dirty trick.That is despite Alaska's ranked-choice voting system making the situation "better for the Republican incumbent," according to David Smith, associate professor of American politics and foreign policy at the University of Sydney's US Studies Centre."If [someone] wanted to vote for Dan Sullivan but didn't know which one to vote for … as long as they put both of them above the Democrat [candidate], then Dan Sullivan is going to end up with the vote," he added."So it's really hard to see how this could unfairly change the election result at all."Democrats accused of ballot stackingAlaska is considered a high-stakes midterms race, and Ms Peltola, a Yup'ik Alaska Native and former congresswoman, hopes it will form part of next week's blue wave predicted by some pollsters.Mary Peltola is running as the Democratic candidate for Alaska's US Senate seat. (AP: Mark Thiessen)If successful, she would become the first Democrat in nearly two decades to represent the state in the Senate."We've seen increasingly … that Democratic candidates seem to be competitive in states that went heavily for Trump in 2024. And Alaska is one of those states," Dr Smith said.But Ms Peltola's campaign was rocked by The New York Times report suggesting that since the summer of 2025, her team had tried to recruit a Dan Sullivan to run for Senate.Elisa Rios, Ms Peltola's former campaign manager and longtime aide, who was fired amid a staff shake-up in August, told the newspaper the DSCC had introduced the Peltola campaign to a political operative and Ohio native named Jerid Kurtz.At a later meeting, this aide said he had recruited a Dan Sullivan who he described as "amenable to running if it would help Ms Peltola", the Times reported.Dan J Sullivan and Ms Peltola did not respond to the ABC's requests for comment.The tactic of selecting rival candidates with the same name to run, referred to as ballot-stacking, has, according to Dr Smith, been used by both parties in the past, and is generally considered legal.Political parties may also seek candidates who appeal to a similar group of voters as the main rival, or stoke confusion to potentially influence the outcome of a close race.Dr Smith said the tactic was used by Republicans during the 2024 campaign in Alaska when the GOP fought to keep another Democrat on the ballot who was actually in prison in New York at the time.Steve Jarding, a former communications director for the DSCC, told top political website The Hill that ballot stacking was normal when he was at the Senate committee in Washington.During a campaign stop in Soldotna on Friday, Ms Peltola labelled the Times report a "distraction"."Mary got in this race because Alaskans deserve a champion who is fighting to lower their costs and put Alaska first, and no tweet or threat from any DC politician will keep her away from that fight," her campaign said.But that hasn't stopped Republicans from seizing on the issue.Trump jumps on election interference allegationsWith the case of the Alaskan Dans making national headlines days out from the midterms, Mr Trump and his attorney-general, Todd Blanche, have begun to ramp up allegations of election interference.Mr Trump has called for Ms Peltola to be criminally prosecuted and removed from the ballot in the Senate race."I think they should be prosecuted. To me, that's voter fraud at the highest level," he told reporters.Donald Trump has directed the DOJ to sue to block certification of the Senate race if the Republicans do not win Alaska. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)The DOJ's lawsuit, filed on Thursday, said Alaska should be prevented from certifying the result if senator Dan Sullivan loses by fewer votes than his namesake receives, pending an investigation.The probe would determine if voters mistakenly supported the wrong Sullivan, though it does not explain how this process would work. Votes are supposed to be confidential."I think name recognition [of] Senator Dan in Alaska is at 100 per cent," said Alaskan veteran political reporter James Brooks."As is name recognition for his leading Democratic challenger. People in Alaska have been inundated with ads, mailers, phone calls, and at this point it's difficult to find anyone who doesn't know what's happening."Dr Smith doubted the DOJ lawsuit would proceed given states mostly run their own elections according to their own laws."Federal Congress can make laws regarding federal elections, but they haven't made any laws about this situation," he said."The fact that the federal government has said that this lawsuit will only apply if Dan Sullivan loses is another thing that makes it completely invalid. The federal government is not supposed to be a partisan entity; it's not supposed to be filing lawsuits on behalf of one candidate."He believed Republicans were using this issue to sow seeds of doubt about the broader mi

sources.headline: Trump calls for Mary Peltola to be banned from Alaska senate race
sources.text: WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump intensified his attacks on Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola following a news report that her allies had secretly recruited candidates to join the state’s US Senate race in order to dilute support for Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.“I think Dan Sullivan – the fake Dan Sullivan – and Mary Peltola should be, number one, they should be taken off the ballot, and number two, they should be prosecuted,” Trump told reporters on Oct 28. There’s no clear legal mechanism for the Democrat’s removal from the race and Trump did not provide direct evidence that her or her campaign advisers broke the law.The New York Times reported on Oct 28 that Peltola’s team engaged in a broad attempt to peel votes from Sullivan by recruiting spoilers into the race.So-called “ballot-stacking” manoeuvres are common in US politics and are generally thought to be legal.In a social media post earlier on Oct 28, Trump called the effort “illegal” and said Peltola should “suffer the legal and political consequences for what she has done”, including her own exclusion from the race. “In Alaska, I don’t think Mary Peltola, after perpetrating such a terrible scheme, should be allowed to run, because this is election fraud,” he said in a subsequent post.Peltola’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Trump’s post.Both her campaign and the Senate Democrats’ campaign arm have denied involvement in the candidate recruitment effort. The plan, dubbed the “ballot composition project”, resulted in the candidacy of retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan, the Times reported.Peltola’s campaign said in a statement that it “has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign”.The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee said in a statement that it, too, “is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan”.Trump’s critics have called his attacks an attempt to nullify an election that could decide control of the Senate.Alaska is one of a number of traditionally Republican states with unexpectedly competitive Senate races, in large part thanks to voters’ dissatisfaction with Trump’s handling of the cost of living.At Trump’s request, the Department of Justice (DOJ) filed a lawsuit seeking to pre-emptively block the certification of Senate election results in Alaska if Senator Sullivan loses by a close margin, citing the risk of “voter confusion” with two individuals on the ballot having similar names.The department argued that Daniel J. Sullivan is running as a deliberate spoiler to Senator Sullivan’s re-election campaign.In a filing on Oct 28 in the federal court in Anchorage, the DOJ said that in the light of the New York Times report, the US intends to quickly seek information from Peltola’s campaign about whether it “attempted to deceive the court by seeking an expedited ruling on a motion to dismiss when the campaign may have been aware of the New York Times reporting before it was published”.Trump last week said he was very concerned about the race, accusing Democrats of “election interference”. BLOOMBERG
